newsitem.title: USA: NYCE, CSCE say NYMEX space offer just commercial.
newsitem.headline: NYCE, CSCE say NYMEX space offer just commercial.

text.p: New York Cotton Exchange said an offer from New York Mercantile Exchange to share space in its new $228 million building overlooking the Hudson River would be on commercial terms and not include any merger overtures.
"As far as we are concerned, we are talking about a commercial relationship," NYCE president Joe O'Neill said.
"I think all the exchanges in New York view being in one building as the ideal, and if it can work, that would be terrific," O'Neill said.

NYMEX has offered 15,000 sq ft of trading space and 35,000 sq ft of office space to NYCE and Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in its new building in Manhattan's Battery Park City, due to be occupied from Memorial Day weekend.
A CSCE spokeswoman said more time was needed to discuss the offer. "We don't have any specifics on space, cost or what it would entail," she said. "But we are very receptive to this."
All three exchanges, including NYMEX's COMEX division, share a floor in the World Trade Center.
NYCE and CSCE exchanges rebuffed NYMEX's $48 million merger offer, made in October 1995.
"The merger offer is still open, but this offer of space is unrelated," a NYMEX spokeswoman said. Financing for the new NYMEX building was already in place.
The offer of space was due to futures commission merchants or FCMs wanting to keep together, NYMEX said.
NYCE and CSCE went ahead some time ago with planning a new trading floor for themselves, also in Manhattan's financial district.
O'Neill said NYCE and CSCE will discuss the space offer.
"Whatever we do, we will make a joint decision," he said.
Construction of NYCE and CSCE's new building had not started, but O'Neill was unable to say how much has been spent on the project to date. There was no penalty clause if that project was scrapped.
NYCE and CSCE's new building would have 25,000 to 30,000 square feet of trading space and 80,000 to 100,000 sq ft of office space.

CSCE and NYCE were persuaded to stay in Manhattan after New York city and state offered an incentive package worth some $90 million to stop them converting a former toothpaste factory over the river in Jersey City.
"There is a lot of common space you don't need to duplicate, but we have to analyse what's available in the new NYMEX building and see what we need," O'Neill said.
NYMEX said there was no deadline on their offer, but the longer NYCE and CSCE mulled the deal, the more difficult it would be to accommodate them.
But if NYMEX gave up some of its space, future expansion plans could also be affected.
"That would have to be an issue to be discussed - what the expansion plans for all the exchanges are going to be," NYMEX said.
((Huw Jones, New York Commodities 212-859-1646))
